items.content:
OpenWorker -- an open source agent that doesn't just chat but completes tasks on your laptop -- just released a new version with many features for security workflows. 

After our initial release, many users found it especially useful for cybersecurity. Attackers are already using AI; OpenWorker is committed to giving defenders the same leverage. Running an agent requires both (i) A model and (ii) A harness (the software around the model). Because the OpenWorker harness is fully open source, security teams can audit it to make sure we haven't built any backdoors that exfiltrate your code and data to some company or even a foreign adversary.

OpenWorker now comes with built-in cybersecurity agents for (i) Scanning your code for vulnerabilities. (ii) Scanning dependencies for supply chain injections. (iii) Checking your cloud security configuration for attack surfaces. This enables developers to do much more security work before deployment (part of what's called the "shift left" movement).

You choose the model: you can run open weight models fully locally so sensitive code never leaves your machine. This helps with legitimate security work (like reproducing a known exploit to defend against it) that can trigger refusals in leading closed models. Or use your ChatGPT subscription, or stealth preview models like Ox Alpha, or any model via API key.

Thanks also to all the open source contributors!

Join work with @rohitcprasad so please follow him too to get more frequent updates.

It really is the GOLDEN AGE of hardware startups.

For basically all of history, hardware was the worst business you cou
items.content:
It really is the GOLDEN AGE of hardware startups.

For basically all of history, hardware was the worst business you could pick. 

You needed a factory, a supply chain, a hardware engineer, tens of millions of dollars, and 2 years before you could even find out if anyone wanted the thing. 

That's why almost nobody did it, and the few who tried mostly died on the manufacturing. 

What's happening now is that every one of those walls is coming down at the same time. 

1. The brains got cheap because open source models can run the thing for basically nothing. 

2. The design got free because the whole robot is open source, so you're not starting from a blank page, you're forking someone else's working robot and changing what you need. 

3. The manufacturing is increasingly something you can contract out in small batches instead of betting the company on a 10 000 unit order.

So now you're able to create a $399 that used to cost like $3999 not long ago.

The thing I keep coming back to is that this is the same pattern software went through, just 15 years later. 

When building an app got cheap, we got a million businesses nobody could have predicted. Building a robot just got cheap. 

I'll add some hardware ideas to https://t.co/a5ARFnvky2 (literally free to sign up to get validated ideas)

TLDR;

We're about to get the same EXPLOSION, except this time it touches the physical world.

I'm not surprised NVDIA agreed to buy HuggingFace for $12.9B. The hardware wave is COMING.

What do you think?

Crazy to me how many people only use AI for single tasks. 

If you're about to do a task and you know you're going to do it more times in the next 2 months, you should instead build the system for that task. 

Ex: you want to launch a paid ad campaign. 

Instead of making the ads from scratch, build an ad factory that allows you to type in the header, style, logo placement, font info, and campaign vibe. Create a review process with the AI.

Instead of pulling the analytics from scratch, build a visibility center that stays updated in real-time and includes an exec summary, a "generate insights", or "generate actions" section. 

Instead of iterating on ads from scratch, grab skills or make one that allows for you to pull ad performance each day, grab the highest performing ads, iterate on them with your ad factory, and spin down the bad performing ones.

items.title:
Putting this tweet in the “scary” category of AI.

Calling upon the non-technical business professionals that follow me
items.content:
Putting this tweet in the “scary” category of AI.

Calling upon the non-technical business professionals that follow me to pay attention. 

I’m breaking down the key parts of the @RyanGreenblatt tweet on the METR research covering the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident.

As background: METR is an independent 3P research non-profit that focuses on AI evaluations and risk assessments. They went to the OpenAI offices for 6 days to run these retros. METR takes no funding from AI companies and was not paid to do this research, but they used ~$400,000 in provided OpenAI credits to complete the research. Ryan is Chief Scientist at Redwood Research, who worked with METR on this, and he was in charge of the transcripts. 

This is a sign of what’s to come. 

1) Scale of understanding massive complex systems requires AI because a human can’t read 1300 transcripts, many with millions of tokens, in a few days - big bottlenecks of time and volume 

2) Humans become more reliant on AI for analysis and explanations of complex AI activity 

3) That process will get harder: 

a) AI may stop communicating in natural language either because it’s less efficient than shorthand code (which they used) or activations (numbers) or because AI agents will want to purposefully hide their reasoning from humans…making it harder to understand. 

b) The incidents may (and almost certainly will) get more complex…making it harder to understand. 

c) AI seems likely to get “smarter” and more capable (ex: better at tool handling, fewer errors, more complex orchestration, more clever at staying stealth or going undetected for longer) and may execute more sophisticated hacks…making it harder to understand. 

d) The AI running the investigation already had issues (incomplete, overconfident) and may be even less helpful in the future and could do more on hiding key details, incomplete answers, lying, or not answering…making it harder to understand. 

Reducing urgency and improving testing and prevention may help. Open reports like this one are also helpful to democratize the details (although, we are also democratizing the details for agents to scan). Seems likely we’ll see more open research in this area.

One of the simplest businesses you can start right now is an agent mystery shopper.

You send an AI agent through a company's site the way a real customer would, and you report back on whether it could finish the job. 

It buys the hoodie from the Shopify store, books the consult at the consulting firm, files the claim at the insurance company. 

Charge $100 to $300 a month per site

Here's the whole setup: 

1) Pick the journeys that actually make the customer money. Checkout, quote request, booking, claims. 

2) Run an agent through each one, on a schedule. 

3) Log every place it stopped: bad descriptions, missing tools, dead ends near the conversion. 

4) Send that report weekly or monthly. That's the product. 

5) Watch which failures show up on every site you test. 

6) Build those fixes into software and sell that too.

Step 6 only works after step 5. You don't know what to build until you've run the same tests across enough sites to see the pattern

It also stacks with anything else you sell. Once you've shown a company the exact point where the agent gave up, telling them WebMCP would fix it isn't a cold pitch. They already saw the failure.
